The active-learning evaluation uses only random and entropy baselines, omitting stronger coreset, diversity, and active fine-tuning methods. Proposed-method curves have no repeated-seed uncertainty or significance analysis, frequently cross targeted entropy, and do not fully support the claim of consistent improvement. Domain-specific validation labels are used for hyperparameter selection and checkpoint selection without being counted in the annotation budget.

Reproducibility and practical-efficiency evidence are inadequate: the main text says that 30,000 pairs were used for Hessian estimation whereas the supplement says 327,680; the stated code link is empty; important prompt, split, seed, Hessian-batch, ECE, and validation details are missing; and no runtime or memory comparison supports the efficiency claim. strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: post-hoc uncertainty quantification for pretrained vision-language models and its use in active data selection.
Restricting a Laplace/KFAC posterior to the projection layers and seeking sampling-free uncertainty propagation is computationally motivated and could be useful if technically corrected.
The evaluation covers two VLM families, five zero-shot datasets, cross-domain active-learning tasks, a larger CLIP variant, and a distance-metric ablation, with accuracy, NLPD, and ECE reported.
The manuscript is generally well organized, uses helpful illustrations, and acknowledges limitations concerning access to pretraining data and proxy-data mismatch.
weaknesses: The central cosine-moment derivation is not valid as written. Equations 56–57 replace the expectation of a ratio by a ratio of expectations even though the numerator and norms are dependent; Equations 61–62 make the analogous unsupported substitution for the second moment. The norm inequality does not justify either step. Moreover, the full covariance produced by Equation 9 is reduced to a diagonal covariance without justification, and the resulting Gaussian has support outside the valid cosine range.

The empirical approximation check exposes an unresolved implementation mismatch: Figures 3 and 5 report quantities labeled cosine similarities with means around 18–31, although cosine similarity must lie in [-1,1]. These may be temperature-scaled logits, but that scaling is absent from the proposed formulas. Validation uses only 500 samples in a small synthetic mean-shift example and provides no quantitative approximation error, coverage, or dataset-level analysis.

Other central Bayesian details are incorrect or incomplete. The marginal-likelihood expression in Equations 27–28 lacks the required log-determinant form; the InfoNCE curvature derivation omits the learned temperature and appears not to account fully for both directions of the symmetric loss; and the generalized-probit mapping from correlated class logits to predictive probabilities is never specified. Consequently, the posterior and probabilities used in the experiments cannot be reconstructed from the paper.

There are numerous consequential internal inconsistencies: the appendix reverses the sign of BALD relative to the correct main-text definition while still selecting the maximum; the online Kronecker updates use n-based weights in Equations 17–18 but square-root weights in Equations 84–85; the Hessian subset is stated as 30,000 examples in the main paper and 327,680 in the supplement; and the pseudo-count search range and whether NLPD is minimized or maximized also conflict. The claimed code URL is blank.

The zero-shot evidence is substantially weaker than claimed. BayesVLM does not consistently outperform temperature scaling or even the uncalibrated models: several accuracy, NLPD, and ECE entries are worse, especially for SigLIP. PCME++ uses a different backbone and training data and has dramatically lower accuracy, so it is not a controlled uncertainty comparison. Missing baselines include Monte Carlo propagation of the same Laplace posterior, which is essential for validating both the analytic approximation and its claimed efficiency.

The active-learning results provide no number of runs, error bars, or significance analysis despite stochastic selection and training. Weighted accuracy is undefined; pool sizes, Monte Carlo settings, and computational costs are missing; only three of the four claimed OfficeHome domains are shown; and method-specific hyperparameters and checkpoints are selected with labeled domain-specific validation data without accounting for that supervision. Several curves are also competitive with, rather than consistently better than, targeted entropy.

Calibration alone does not establish reliable epistemic uncertainty. The paper lacks selective-risk, error-detection, OOD-detection, or coverage evaluations, and interpretability is supported by only one corrupted example. Runtime and memory are not measured despite the efficiency claim, while the method requires hundreds of thousands of pretraining examples and labeled proxy data. These issues, together with the invalid central derivation, leave the main uncertainty and safety-critical claims unsupported.

weaknesses: The central cosine-similarity derivation is not mathematically valid as written. Equations 56 and 62 replace expectations of ratios by ratios of expectations, despite dependence between each embedding and its norm. The formulas also assume diagonal covariance although the preceding matrix-normal posterior generally yields a dense B^{-1}. The reported 'cosine similarities' in Figures 3 and 5 substantially exceed the valid range [-1,1], and the reported variance can exceed one. strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: obtaining post-hoc uncertainty estimates for large vision-language models without modifying their architecture.

weaknesses: The central cosine-moment derivation is not mathematically justified. Equation 56 replaces an expectation of a ratio by a ratio of expectations; Equations 59 and 62 then substitute bounds or expected norms as though they yielded the desired moments. The diagonal-covariance assumption is also unexplained because the preceding Laplace construction generally produces a dense output covariance. Consequently, the claimed analytical mean and variance are heuristics without error bounds or adequate validation.

Figures 3 and 5 label quantities as cosine similarities despite values far outside [-1,1] (approximately -10 to 30 and 17.77 to 30.66), while Figure 5 reports variance as high as 1.16. These cannot be moments of a cosine similarity. If they are temperature-scaled logits, this is neither defined nor reconciled with the derivation.

Several further mathematical and procedural inconsistencies make the method difficult to reproduce: the displayed marginal-likelihood expression is not the standard Laplace evidence; Appendix Equation 72 reverses the BALD sign; the online Kronecker updates differ between the main text and appendix; and the text factor in Equation 24 uses the image encoder notation.

Experimental specifications conflict materially. The main text reports 30,000 samples for Hessian estimation whereas the appendix reports 327,680; the pseudo-count search ends at 50 in the main text but at 200 in the appendix, with the reported SigLIP optimum at 100. The promised code URL is blank, and prompt templates, ECE binning, acquisition sampling details, seeds, and precise data splits are missing.

The zero-shot evidence does not support the stated consistent superiority. BayesVLM loses to temperature scaling on several CLIP NLPD/ECE entries, worsens SigLIP ECE on Flowers-102 and Food-101, and changes accuracy negligibly. PCME++ is evaluated with a different backbone/checkpoint, confounding that comparison, while directly relevant probabilistic-adapter and stronger calibration baselines are absent.

The active-learning evaluation is insufficiently controlled. It uses the complete query/test inputs transductively, and much of the gain comes from k-NN targeting itself. Comparisons are limited mainly to random and entropy selection, with no strong diversity, core-set, or VLM-specific active-learning methods. Seed counts and uncertainty across selection/fine-tuning runs are not reported, despite visibly noisy curves and per-domain hyperparameter tuning.

Approximation quality is assessed using only 500 samples for one input with artificial mean shifts, and interpretability is argued from one corrupted example. There is no quantitative comparison against Monte Carlo propagation across real data, no ablation of the independence and covariance approximations, and no selective-prediction or OOD evaluation to substantiate the safety-critical claims.

The efficiency and training-free framing is not demonstrated: the approach requires access to hundreds of thousands of pretraining examples, Hessian estimation, marginal-likelihood optimization, and labeled proxy data for pseudo-count tuning, yet provides no runtime, memory, or accuracy-versus-cost comparison. Overall, the idea has merit, but the technical flaws and inconclusive evaluation place it clearly below the acceptance threshold.
